title.en: Animated signals are a timing claim

summary: If a scene animates a signal moving along a wire, either model the delay or say the motion is illustrative.
objective: Keep pleasing signal animations from implying a timing model that does not exist.
applies_when: Pulses, glows or particles travel along connections to show activity.
The scene discusses speed, latency, critical path or race conditions.
Several paths of different length are animated together.
example_prompts: Animate the adder carrying and show which path takes longest.
Make the signal flow visible without pretending it is timed.
negative_signals: Static logic views with no motion.
Scenes where the animation is explicitly decorative and labelled as such.
not_for: Static logic views with no motion.
Scenes where the animation is explicitly decorative and labelled as such.

principles: Motion along a wire encodes time. A viewer will read the arrival order and the speed as information whether or not the author intended it.

There is a real quantity available: the propagation delay of a combinational circuit corresponds to the longest path from inputs to outputs, so a scene that wants to talk about speed has something concrete to model.

Logical depth is not delay. Under an equal-delay abstraction, arrival order follows gate count, but with real per-element delays two gates of one unit each and a single gate of two units arrive together, correctly. Animate from summed modelled delays, and if you have no delay model, say the motion shows connectivity.
The honest options are symmetrical: model per-element delay and derive the animation from it, or state that the motion shows connectivity rather than timing.
implementation: If timing is part of the message, give each element a delay, propagate arrival times through the graph and drive the animation from the computed times.
Highlight the longest path explicitly rather than leaving the viewer to infer it from motion.
If timing is not modelled, keep the animation uniform and label it as showing connectivity or activity.

Keep readouts labeled settled consistent with the steady evaluator. If transient values are displayed, label them and derive them from the declared delay model at the selected time; they may differ from the settled result until propagation completes.
State the units of any displayed delay, and mark values as illustrative when they are not from a device model.
observable_checks: Compare arrival times against the summed modelled delays along each path, not against gate counts. Simultaneous arrival on paths of different depth is a fault only under an equal-delay abstraction; with unequal element delays it can be exactly right.

Pause mid-animation and confirm the reported values match what the model says for that moment: a settled readout must match the evaluator, while an explicitly labelled transient view may legitimately differ from the settled values until the modelled delays have elapsed.
Confirm the claimed longest path matches the computed one after an edit.
Check that any displayed delay carries units and a source or an illustrative label.

creative_affordances: Expressive signal effects remain welcome; they simply need an accurate caption.
A deliberately slowed, exaggerated propagation is an excellent teaching device when labelled.
known_limits: Authored guidance citing the definition of propagation delay; it asserts no delay values for any real technology.
It does not model glitches, hazards or analogue edge behaviour.

claims.statement: The propagation delay of a combinational circuit corresponds to the longest path from inputs to outputs through the circuit.
claims.scope: Digital combinational timing at the level of gate-delay counting; it does not give physical delay values or account for hazards.
